The ancient White Temple ziggurat, built for the sky god Anu, still stood nearby as a weathered ruin. Uruk's population had shrunk to a remnant clustered around this one working sanctuary.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Uruk archaeological site at Warka, Iraq, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Nippur never held a king's throne but anchored Mesopotamia's religious life for millennia as the sacred seat of the storm god Enlil. Its Ekur temple complex had crumbled into a twenty-meter mound by the time Trajan's forces campaigned through Babylonia in 116 CE. Sumerian and Babylonian kings alike had claimed legitimacy only after winning Enlil's blessing here. By the Parthian era, Nippur's population had thinned to almost nothing, leaving a landmark ruin.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Interior Gateway of the 19th-Century Excavation Shelter atop Nippur's Ziggurat.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the 19th-century excavation shelter atop Nippur's ziggurat mound, Wikimedia Commons, photo by Noemi Alzayadi

properties.notes: Trajan reached Charax Spasinou in 116 CE and watched merchant ships cast off for India, reportedly weeping that he was too old to follow Alexander's path east. The port sat at the head of the Persian Gulf as capital of Characene, a Parthian vassal kingdom that grew rich taxing trade between Mesopotamia and the Indian Ocean. King Attambelos of Characene submitted to Trajan without a fight, keeping his throne under nominal Roman overlordship. Rome's grip on the port evaporated within the year.

properties.modern_location: near Kufa, Najaf Governorate, Iraq (approximate, unexcavated)
properties.notes: Parthian king Vologases I founded Vologesias on a Euphrates canal south of Babylon to draw trade away from the Greek city of Seleucia. By Trajan's invasion the new town had absorbed much of Seleucia's commerce, becoming one of Parthia's busiest inland ports. Its exact ruins remain unidentified today, buried somewhere near the later Islamic city of Kufa. Vologesias stayed under Parthian control throughout Trajan's campaign, never falling within the short-lived Roman province.

Roman troops briefly held Dura-Europos in 114 CE, raising a triumphal arch to Trajan outside its walls before withdrawing. An inscription from 117 CE records a priest restoring a temple whose doors Roman soldiers had removed, proof the garrison was gone by Trajan's death. The fortified caravan city sat ninety meters above the Euphrates and had changed hands between Parthian and Roman rule for generations. It fell under Parthian control again by mid-117, decades before Rome annexed it in 165 CE.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of Dura-Europos overlooking the Euphrates, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Trajan's forces captured Nisibis in 115 CE, and the city anchored his short-lived province of Mesopotamia. Positioned at the foot of the Tur Abdin mountains, Nisibis had already changed hands between Armenian, Parthian, and Roman rule for generations before Roman troops arrived. Hadrian abandoned the province within two years of Trajan's death, though Nisibis returned to Roman hands repeatedly over the following two centuries. Its fame as a Christian learning center still lay ahead.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Mar Jacob church at the site of ancient Nisibis, a later Christian-era structure marking the location, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Trajan's general Lusius Quietus seized Singara around 114 CE, folding the caravan town at the foot of Mount Sinjar into Rome's new Mesopotamian frontier. The city guarded a key crossing on the trade route linking Nisibis to the Tigris and later garrisoned an entire Roman legion, the First Parthica. In 117 CE Singara remained a fresh, uncertain Roman outpost, months from the abandonment Hadrian ordered after Trajan's death. Its full legionary fortification came later, under Severus.

Trajan's forces completed the conquest of Adiabene in 116 CE by building a pontoon bridge over the Tigris and capturing Arbela, the kingdom's capital. The city's citadel already sat atop more than five thousand years of continuous settlement, among the oldest continuously inhabited places on earth. Adiabene's king had until then balanced loyalty between Parthia and Rome from this hilltop stronghold. Roman rule lasted barely two years before Hadrian released the territory back to local control.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Erbil Citadel, Erbil, Kurdistan Region of Iraq.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the Erbil Citadel, site of ancient Arbela, Wikimedia Commons, photo by MSinjari, CC BY-SA 3.0

properties.notes: Nebuchadnezzar II built Borsippa's ziggurat as a twin to Babylon's own tower, dedicating it to the god Nabu eighteen kilometers southwest of Babylon. A lightning strike had already fused its upper brickwork into vitrified glass-like slag centuries before Trajan's army passed nearby in 116 CE. Early modern travelers mistook the fire-scarred ruin, known locally as Birs Nimrud, for the biblical Tower of Babel itself. Nabu's temple beside it drew only sporadic offerings by then.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/The ruins of the Ziggurat of Nabu at Borsippa, Iraq.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the ruins of the ziggurat of Nabu at Borsippa, Iraq, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sargon II built Dur-Sharrukin from nothing as his new capital, finishing the entire walled city within a single decade before 706 BCE. His unexpected death in battle the following year doomed the city, as his son Sennacherib abandoned it for Nineveh and never looked back. By Trajan's Assyrian campaign of 116 CE the capital had lain empty for more than eight centuries, its colossal winged bull guardians buried under windblown sand. Roman soldiers left no record of the buried city.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Lamassu inscription 1 - Palace of Sargon II, Khorsabad - Oriental Institute Museum, University of Chicago - DSC07526.JPG?width=800
properties.image_credit: Photograph of a lamassu from the Palace of Sargon II at Khorsabad (Dur-Sharrukin), Oriental Institute Museum, University of Chicago, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Sumerian tradition named Kish the first city to hold kingship after a great flood, a claim recorded on the ancient Sumerian King List. Its Neo-Babylonian ziggurat, raised under Nebuchadnezzar II, still rose above the plain when Trajan's forces campaigned through Babylonia in 116 CE, though the city itself lay largely abandoned. Kish's ruins sprawl across forty scattered mounds east of Babylon. Occupation had faded to almost nothing, leaving only the ziggurat as a landmark.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Ruins of the ziggurat of the ancient city of Kish, Tell al-Uhaymir, Iraq.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the ziggurat ruins of Kish at Tell al-Uhaymir, Iraq, Wikimedia Commons, photo by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin, CC BY-SA 4.0

properties.modern_location: Tell as-Senkereh, Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
properties.notes: Larsa's kings once rivaled Babylon itself, ruling southern Mesopotamia from the throne of Rim-Sin before Hammurabi conquered the city in 1763 BCE. Its Ebabbar temple to the sun god Shamash had functioned for over a thousand years, among the longest-running religious institutions in Mesopotamian history. By the time Trajan's campaign reached Babylonia in 116 CE, Larsa's settlement had faded away, its temple mound reduced to a scarred ruin southeast of Uruk.

properties.modern_location: Abu Shahrain, Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
properties.notes: Sumerian myth named Eridu the very first city, founded by the water god Enki before the gods created any other place on earth. Archaeologists found fourteen successive temples stacked atop one another at Eridu's shrine, each generation rebuilding on its predecessor's ruins. By Trajan's Parthian War the city had been abandoned for over a millennium, its ziggurat mound a bare, wind-scoured hill. No Roman source records a visit to Mesopotamia's oldest ruined city.
properties.image_credit: Photograph of the ziggurat ruins at Eridu, Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Tell Telloh, Dhi Qar Governorate, Iraq
properties.notes: Governor Gudea rebuilt Girsu as a showcase capital around 2100 BCE, commissioning more than twenty diorite statues of himself for its temples. The city served as capital of the Lagash city-state and center of worship for the war god Ningirsu, whose temple Eninnu Gudea rebuilt with stone hauled from as far as Lebanon. By Trajan's campaign through Babylonia in 116 CE, Girsu had lain buried and forgotten for nearly two thousand years. French excavators only rediscovered it in 1877.
properties.image_credit: Statue of Gudea, ruler of Lagash, excavated at Girsu, Louvre Museum. Wikimedia Commons.

properties.modern_location: Tell Abu Habbah, Baghdad Governorate, Iraq
properties.notes: Sippar served as Mesopotamia's chief cult center for the sun god Shamash, its Ebabbar temple drawing worship for more than a thousand years. Excavators recovered tens of thousands of cuneiform tablets from the site's scribal archives, among the largest caches ever found in Mesopotamia. Occupation continued at a reduced level into the Parthian period, though by Trajan's campaign of 116 CE the once-great temple city had shrunk to a minor settlement near the Euphrates.
properties.image_credit: Tablet of Shamash, limestone relief recovered from Sippar, British Museum. Wikimedia Commons.
